title: Avoiding Three Midlife Risk Factors Could Delay Dementia by 13 Years
excerpt: Not smoking, controlling blood pressure, and managing diabetes in your 50s could add nearly 13 dementia-free years, a 26-year study of more than 12,000 adults found.
body:
• Not smoking, having normal blood pressure, and no diabetes in midlife was associated with nearly 13 additional dementia-free years, a 26-year study of 12,409 U.S. adults found.
  • Participants with all three risk factors were 2.7 times more likely to develop dementia and over five times more likely to die prematurely.
  • By age 85, only 7% of adults with all three risk factors remained dementia-free, compared with 35% of those with none.
  • The findings carry particular weight for South Asians, who face elevated rates of diabetes and hypertension — two of the three factors identified.

People who avoid smoking, high blood pressure, and diabetes during middle age can expect to live nearly 13 years longer without dementia than those who have all three risk factors, according to a study published on August 5 in Neurology Open Access.

The research, led by Dr. Josef Coresh at NYU Langone Health, analyzed data from 12,409 participants in the Atherosclerosis Risk in Communities (ARIC) study, a community-based project that has tracked adults from four U.S. communities since the late 1980s. Participants were 56 years old on average and free of dementia at baseline. Over a median follow-up of 26 years, 3,008 developed dementia and 5,238 died without developing the condition.

The Numbers Behind the Headline

The difference was stark. Participants with none of the three vascular risk factors lived an average of 30.1 dementia-free years after the study began, compared with 17.5 years for those with all three — a gap of 12.6 years.

Those with all three risk factors were 2.7 times more likely to develop dementia and more than five times more likely to die prematurely from another cause. By age 85, only 7% of participants with all three risk factors remained dementia-free, compared with 35% of those with none.

"Our findings argue that people need to actively avert these factors in midlife as a strategy for preserving brain health for more than a decade."

— Dr. Josef Coresh, Founding Director, Optimal Aging Institute, NYU Langone

Women lived longer without dementia than men regardless of how many risk factors they had. Women with all three risk factors lived an average of 18.1 dementia-free years, compared with 16.6 years for men in the same group.

How Vascular Damage Harms the Brain

Smoking, uncontrolled blood pressure, and diabetes share a common mechanism: they damage blood vessels throughout the body, including those that supply the brain. Over time, this reduces the delivery of oxygen and nutrients and increases the risk of stroke and small vessel disease, making the brain more vulnerable to cognitive decline.

"The way we live has the most profound impact, and I'm talking about a magnitude that is unachievable by any medication," said Dr. Andrew Freeman, director of cardiovascular prevention and wellness at National Jewish Health in Denver, who was not involved in the study.

About 45% of dementia cases globally are attributed to modifiable risk factors, according to Dr. Sanjula Singh, an assistant professor in neurology at Harvard Medical School. These include not only the three factors in this study but also high cholesterol, physical inactivity, hearing loss, depression, and social isolation.

What This Means for South Asians

The findings carry particular urgency for South Asian communities. Research has consistently shown that South Asians face elevated rates of type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular disease compared with other ethnic groups — two of the three risk factors the study identified as most damaging to long-term brain health.

India alone is estimated to have over 8.8 million people living with dementia, a number projected to rise sharply as the population ages. For diaspora communities in the U.S., U.K., and Canada, where access to healthcare is more readily available, the study reinforces that midlife is the critical window for intervention.

What You Can Do

The practical steps are straightforward: quit smoking, manage blood pressure, and control blood sugar. A plant-based diet such as the DASH (Dietary Approaches to Stop Hypertension) plan, regular physical activity, adequate sleep, and stress management all help address these risks. Regular health checkups to monitor blood pressure and blood sugar levels are essential, especially from your 40s onward.

The study has limitations. It shows an association, not causation, and risk factors were measured only once during midlife. "View the results as an important estimate rather than the exact prediction for every individual," Singh said. But Coresh emphasized that the framework of years gained, rather than abstract percentages, makes the case easier for clinicians and patients to act on.

"Discovering new ways to delay dementia is crucial, with 42% of Americans at risk for developing the condition at any time after age 55," Coresh said.
